content: 1. Identify risks and risk factors as quickly as possible to prevent or minimize harm. 2. Conduct pre-transmission assessment surveys (pre-TAS) and follow-up assessments at sentinel and spot-check sites after five effective rounds of mass drug administration (MDA). 3. An implementation unit (IU) passes pre-TAS if the prevalence of infection is reduced to less than 1% microfilaraemia or less than 2% antigenaemia in sentinel and spot-check sites. 4. If pre-TAS is passed, the IU may proceed to the transmission assessment survey (TAS). 5. A sentinel site is a geographical area with a population of at least 500 people, selected to collect parasitological data for monitoring the success of the program. The same site should be used throughout the program. 6. Sentinel site assessments, along with spot-check site assessments, are conducted at baseline, mid-term (optional), and during the pre-TAS survey. 7. Serious adverse events (SAEs) following MDA include any medical occurrence that results in death, requires hospitalization or prolongation of an existing hospital stay, causes persistent or significant disability or incapacity, or is life-threatening. Cancers, congenital anomalies, or birth defects are also considered serious. Events that would have been serious without acute treatment should also be classified as SAEs. 8. In reviewed studies, any Grade 4 or 5 adverse event or any overnight admission to a health facility was considered an SAE. These were designated as critical outcomes in the recommendation formulation process. 9. A spot-check site is a geographical area with a population of at least 500 people, selected to complement data collected at sentinel sites. Spot-check sites are chosen for each assessment and may change over the course of the program. 10. Spot-check sites and sentinel sites are assessed at baseline, mid-term, and during the pre-TAS survey. 11. Surveillance involves the ongoing, systematic collection and evaluation of data describing the occurrence and spread of disease. It also includes efforts to discover, investigate, and eliminate ongoing transmission, prevent and treat infections, and substantiate the claimed absence of transmission. 12. The target population for lymphatic filariasis (LF) elimination is the eligible population within an implementation unit, typically 80–90% of the total population, based on drug safety criteria. 13. The transmission assessment survey (TAS) is designed to determine whether evaluation units have reduced infection prevalence to a level where recrudescence is unlikely, even without MDA interventions. TAS is a decision-making tool to determine when MDA can be stopped. 14. Validation of LF elimination as a public health problem involves documenting the elimination process and submitting a validation dossier to WHO for approval. Validation is not a permanent state and does not signify the end of program activities. Post-validation surveillance and minimum care for patients must continue within the healthcare system. 15. The World Health Organization (WHO) acknowledges the contributions of numerous professionals who dedicated their time, expertise, and knowledge to the development and review of this guideline. 16. The guideline development group was chaired by Margaret Gyapong, a social scientist from Ghana, and co-chaired by Mohammed Toseef Ansari, a GRADE methodologist from Canada. The group included experts in epidemiology, parasitology, immunology, health economics, and other fields from various countries. 17. External peer reviewers provided valuable input on the final guideline document. These reviewers included medical epidemiologists, parasitologists, and public health policy advisors from institutions worldwide. 18. Systematic review contributors coordinated the reviews, developed evidence profiles, and conducted statistical analyses. The team was led by Xavier Bosch-Capblanch from the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute. 19. The guideline was developed in accordance with WHO procedures and the WHO handbook for guideline development. A steering committee was formed to develop PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome) questions and refine the scope of the guideline. 20. A systematic review team conducted a systematic review, meta-analysis, and critical appraisal of the evidence. Recommendations were formulated using the GRADE approach during a meeting in Geneva in May 2017. 21. Two alternative MDA regimens for LF elimination were developed in response to countries requesting WHO to devise new strategies to realign their national programs toward elimination. 22. WHO guidelines are documents containing recommendations about health interventions, whether clinical, public health, or policy-related. These guidelines are approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. 23. The Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF) was launched by WHO in 2000 with the goal of achieving global elimination of LF as a public health problem by 2020. 24. The elimination strategy includes annual MDA to interrupt transmission and morbidity management to alleviate suffering. 25. Despite progress, some endemic countries have not started MDA in all implementation units, and others face suboptimal assessment results after completing five effective MDA rounds. 26. The guideline serves as a response to these challenges, providing alternative regimens to help countries achieve elimination goals. 27. Funding for the guideline was provided by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), but the development and content were completed independently of the funder.
